newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia's Politika group IPO fully subscribed.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia's Politika group IPO fully subscribed.

text.p: Yugoslavia's largest news and publishing company Politika, waving goodbye to 50 years of Communist ideology, has restored shareholding after its entire first privatisation issue was fully subscribed.
"This is fantastic...the result I could not possibly have dreamed of," said Politika general manager Hadzi Dragan Antic, calling privatisation an irrevocable process.

"This is the first real privatisation in Yugoslavia. The case of Politika is very complex. This is an end to one ideology and for the first time, Politika has very clearly defined owners," Antic told Reuters in an interview.
In December, Politika invited investors to buy 510,000 shares in its first privatisation issue, representing about 10 percent of its total capital.

The shares, each of 100 German marks face value, were sold at par under local laws, raising 51 million marks ($31.1 million) to kick off a privatisation process combining a debt-to-equity swap and sale of shares.
"Politika's privatisation is very important. It is a huge responsibility. Everybody will look at us to see whether the model works and brings quality," Antic said.
Federal Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, adopted a new non-compulsory privatisation law last July, but envisaged no deadline for the process.

Re-establishing itself as a shareholding company, its original status when founded in 1904, and taking France's Le Monde as a model, Politika AD opted for a model of three groups of shareholders with equal stakes in the company.
The first was original shareholders, their heirs and the employees, the state and state companies were the second and the third was all other investors.
To indemnify original shareholders who suffered damages with a 1946 nationalisation law, Politika decided to return what rightfully belonged to them.

The Ribnikar family, founder of the daily Politika, and two other founding families, received 11 million marks, worth of shares. They and the state with its banks and funds were major shareholders in 1946.

"It was possible to return to the Ribnikars what belonged to them only due to an ingenious legal invention of good will. Thus Politika was able to compensate them even though there is no denationalisation law yet," Antic said.

"This is a historical moment and if somebody tried to revoke the process it would produce a situation much worse than the one we witness on the streets at the moment," he said, referring to pro-democracy demonstrations.
Around 2,000 employees have subscribed a total of six million marks in shares. Together with the original shareholders, they will control a stake of some 170 million marks in the company, Antic said.
In the debt-to-equity swap, two state monopolies -- posts and telecommunications company PTT Srbija and NIS oil industry -- each subscribed 10 percent of issued shares.
Politika allows its employees to pay their stake fully in 60 monthly instalments. The state and other investors have 12 months to complete payment.

Even though the payment of a dividend was not planned after the first year, Antic expected Politika would manage to pay first dividends in February 1998. "Dividend will be proportional to the size of paid capital."

The company, running the biggest circulation daily in Yugoslavia, two printing works and 1,300 sales outlets, said there were plenty of opportunities to privatise, and planned another share issue later this year after issue of a privatisation law.
Politika also planned to list its shares soon at the Belgrade bourse and to seek listing on the London Stock Exchange in one year's time, Antic said.
-- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
($ = 1.640 German Marks)
